title: Liberal Order vs. Multipolarity
scope: The US-led rules-based order versus an emerging multipolar world.

overview.summary: Whether the US-led order built after 1945 is ending or only strained, whom it serves, and what world order should come next.
overview.scope_covered: Whether the US-led order is ending or under strain, what it delivered, what a world of several great powers would be like, and what the United States, its allies, China, Russia and the Global South want instead.
overview.scope_excluded: Humanitarian intervention, nuclear weapons policy, trade policy as such and democratic backsliding, each on its own page; the wars in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran and the Taiwan question appear only as evidence.
overview.why_now: Opening the UN General Assembly’s annual debate on September 22, 2026, Secretary-General António Guterres told world leaders, “We are clearly moving towards a multipolar world. And that movement is irreversible,” and warned it could bring either fragmentation or shared rules.

stats.label: Share of world GDP at purchasing power parity, 2000 and 2025
stats.note: At purchasing power parity, China produced about 19.6 percent of world output in 2025 and the United States 14.6, against 6.7 and 20.4 in 2000; at market exchange rates the order reverses.
stats.detail: Purchasing power parity converts each economy at what goods and services actually cost locally rather than at market exchange rates, so it counts what an economy can produce and buy at home, including soldiers, steel and construction. On this measure China passed the United States in the IMF’s figures in the mid-2010s, and India is now the third-largest economy. The same database shows the advanced economies as a group falling from about 58 percent of world output in 2000 to about 39 percent in 2025, and emerging and developing economies rising from about 42 to about 61 percent. Those who see a multipolar world already here usually cite this measure. It says less about what an economy can buy abroad, such as advanced chips, aircraft or foreign debt, which is why the market-exchange-rate measure tells a different story. The 2025 values are IMF estimates from the April 2026 World Economic Outlook and will be revised slightly in later editions.
stats.source_label: IMF, World Economic Outlook database (April 2026), GDP based on PPP, share of world

stats.label: Armed conflicts involving a state, 2025
stats.note: Uppsala recorded 65 armed conflicts with a government on at least one side in 2025, the most since its records begin in 1946; eight were between states, also a record.
stats.detail: The Uppsala Conflict Data Program at Uppsala University is the most widely used source of conflict data. It counts an armed conflict when organized fighting involving at least one government causes at least 25 battle-related deaths in a year, and a war at 1,000 or more. In 2025 it counted 13 wars, the most since 1992, and about 244,600 people killed in organized violence of all kinds, the second-deadliest year since the Rwandan genocide in 1994. Conflicts between states doubled for the second year running; they include Russia–Ukraine, Iran–Israel, India–Pakistan and Israel–Syria. UCDP’s senior analyst Shawn Davies attributes the rise to “increased international tensions and changes in the global security order.” Liberal internationalists read the trend as the cost of a weakening order; others note that most conflicts are civil wars, many of which began during the years of US primacy.
stats.source_label: Uppsala Conflict Data Program, Uppsala University, release of June 9, 2026 (via EurekAlert)

stats.label: Share of world GDP at market exchange rates, 1990 and 2025
stats.note: Measured in dollars at market exchange rates, the United States produced about 26 percent of world output in 2025, almost exactly its 1990 share; China rose from under 2 percent to about 17.
stats.detail: This is the measure usually cited by those who argue the United States remains the dominant power. At market prices the US share rose to about 30 percent around 2000, fell to about 22 percent by 2010 as China and the euro boomed, and recovered to about 26 percent as US growth outpaced Europe and Japan. Most of the fall in the West’s share at market prices since 1990 is the relative decline of Europe and Japan. China’s dollar share has hovered around 16 to 18 percent since about 2020. The shares are computed for this page from the IMF’s dollar GDP figures: $30.8 trillion for the United States and $19.6 trillion for China in 2025, out of a world total of $118.2 trillion. Market exchange rates swing with currency movements, so single-year comparisons can mislead.
stats.source_label: IMF, World Economic Outlook database (April 2026), GDP in current US dollars; shares computed for this page

stats.label: Share of world foreign-exchange reserves held in US dollars
stats.note: At the end of March 2026, 57.13 percent of official reserves whose currency is reported were held in US dollars, against 20.03 percent in euros and 1.99 percent in renminbi.
stats.detail: Central banks hold reserves in currencies they trust to keep their value and to be usable in a crisis, so the dollar’s share is a standard gauge of confidence in the US-centered financial system. The share rose from 56.42 percent at the end of 2025, which the IMF attributes mainly to the dollar’s mild appreciation against major currencies; quarter-to-quarter moves are dominated by exchange-rate swings. The yen held 5.44 percent, and the smaller currencies grouped as “other” 6.18 percent, out of total reserves of $13.10 trillion. The IMF notes that in 2025 gold overtook US Treasuries as a share of total official reserves, and attributes that almost entirely to the rise in the gold price.
stats.source_label: IMF, Data Brief: Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves, First Quarter of 2026 (July 1, 2026)

stats.label: Military spending by country, 2025
stats.note: The United States spent $954 billion on its military in 2025, a third of the world total and 2.8 times SIPRI’s estimate for China; Chinese and Russian figures are estimates.
stats.detail: World military spending rose for the 11th year in a row in 2025, by 2.9 percent in real terms, to $2,887 billion, the highest SIPRI has recorded and 2.5 percent of world GDP. US spending fell 7.5 percent, in part because no supplemental appropriations for military aid to Ukraine or Israel were allocated in 2025, while China’s rose 7.4 percent, Russia’s 5.9 percent, Germany’s 24 percent and Europe’s as a whole 14 percent. The US share of world spending fell 4.3 percentage points in one year, and the ratio of US to Chinese spending fell from 3.2 times in 2024. The 32 NATO members together spent $1,581 billion, 55 percent of the world total. The Chinese, Russian, Ukrainian and Saudi figures are SIPRI estimates, since China and Russia do not publish full data, and dollar comparisons understate what China and Russia buy at local prices. Those who see US primacy intact point to the lead and the alliance network; those who see multipolarity point to the narrowing gap, China’s naval buildup and rearmament in Europe and Asia.
stats.source_label: SIPRI, Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2025 (Fact Sheet, April 2026)

stats.label: International bodies the United States ordered itself out of, January 2026
stats.note: On January 7, 2026, President Trump directed the United States to withdraw from 66 international organizations, 31 of them UN entities and 35 outside the UN.
stats.detail: The White House said the bodies “operate contrary to U.S. national interests, security, economic prosperity, or sovereignty.” According to JURIST’s summary of the memorandum, the list includes the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, UN Women, the International Law Commission and the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance. It followed orders in 2025 to leave the World Health Organization, the UN Human Rights Council and UNESCO. Supporters, such as the Heritage Foundation, see the withdrawals as reclaiming sovereignty and money from bodies that oppose US interests; critics see the United States leaving the field to China. The United States remains in the UN itself, NATO, the IMF, the World Bank and the WTO.
stats.source_label: The White House, Fact Sheet, January 7, 2026

stats.label: Favorable views of the United States and China abroad, 2023 to 2026
stats.note: Across 20 countries Pew has surveyed every year since 2023, the median favorable view of the United States fell from 58 to 36 percent by 2026, while China’s rose from 32 to 46.
stats.detail: Respondents were asked whether they have a favorable or unfavorable opinion of each country; the 2026 survey was fielded from February 8 to May 13. The 20 countries are Canada, Mexico, Brazil and Argentina, eight in Europe, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia and Australia, and Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa. In the full 36-country 2026 survey, China was viewed more favorably than the United States in 25 countries and the United States more favorably in six, including India, Japan, the Philippines, South Korea and Israel. The United States still leads on a different question: a 36-country median of 39 percent say the US government respects its people’s personal freedoms, against 26 percent for China. Pew’s companion report on views of China finds a 37-country median of 51 percent favorable.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, “People in Many Countries Now View China More Positively Than the U.S.” (July 2026)

stats.label: Share of foreign-exchange trades with the US dollar on one side
stats.note: The dollar was on one side of 89.2 percent of all foreign-exchange trades in April 2025, up from 88.4 percent in 2022; the renminbi was on one side of 8.5 percent.
stats.detail: Every currency trade involves two currencies, so shares add up to 200 percent, not 100: the euro was on one side of 28.9 percent of trades, the yen 16.8 and sterling 10.2. The dollar’s share has been close to 90 percent in every survey for decades because most trades between two other currencies are routed through it. The renminbi has risen steadily since 2013, to fifth place, and trading in the dollar–renminbi pair rose sharply between 2022 and 2025. The BIS notes that turnover in April 2025 was boosted by market turbulence after US tariff announcements. Those who argue that financial power has shifted far less than economic output cite this and the reserve figures; the dollar plumbing of world finance is also what gives US sanctions their reach.
stats.source_label: Bank for International Settlements, Triennial Central Bank Survey: OTC foreign exchange turnover in April 2025

stats.label: Share of world GDP at purchasing power parity, G7 and the ten BRICS members
stats.note: The ten BRICS members produced about 39 percent of world output at purchasing power parity in 2025, up from about 21 percent in 2000; the G7’s share fell from about 45 to about 28.
stats.detail: The G7 is Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States. BRICS is counted as its ten confirmed members: Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, plus Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia, which joined in 2024 and 2025. Saudi Arabia was invited and attends but has not confirmed membership; adding it brings the total to about 40.5 percent. The totals are sums of the IMF’s country shares, computed for this page. The crossover is the headline statistic of the multipolar case. China alone is about half of the BRICS total, and the bloc’s members disagree on much: India and China have an unresolved border dispute, and Iran, the UAE and Egypt sit on opposite sides of several Middle East conflicts.
stats.source_label: IMF, World Economic Outlook database (April 2026), GDP based on PPP, share of world; group totals computed for this page

stats.label: Economies that trade more with China than with the United States, 2023
stats.note: In 2023, 145 of 205 economies traded more with China than with the United States, and China was the largest trading partner of 60 economies against 33 for the United States.
stats.detail: When China joined the WTO in 2001, more than 80 percent of economies traded more with the United States than with China. By 2018 the pattern had reversed, with 139 of 202 economies trading more with China, and it held through 2023. The more recent change is intensity: 112 economies traded more than twice as much with China as with America in 2023, up from 92 in 2018. The Lowy Institute authors add that the relationship is lopsided. Almost 80 percent of economies imported more from China than from the United States, but the United States was still the larger export market for more than half of all economies, because China buys comparatively little from the rest of the world. Trade weight gives China leverage, and its role as a supplier more than a customer is the main reason others say that leverage has limits.
stats.source_label: Lowy Institute, Roland Rajah and Ahmed Albayrak, “China versus America on global trade” (January 2025)

stats.label: Security Council vetoes since 1946, by permanent member
stats.note: Of the 320 vetoes cast from 1946 through 2025, 155 were by the Soviet Union or Russia and 94 by the United States; two cast in private meetings are left out of the members’ totals.
stats.detail: Each of the five permanent members of the Security Council, the victors of 1945, can block any binding Council decision, which makes the Council the clearest case of the 1945 power structure written into law. Veto use was lowest in the 1990s, with 10 vetoed draft resolutions. It has risen since: 47 vetoes were cast on 37 drafts between 2015 and 2024, against 36 vetoes on 30 drafts from 1990 to 2014. Russia vetoed all 18 vetoed drafts on Syria since 2011, with China joining on 10, and 15 of China’s vetoes have come since 2007, all alongside Russia; China’s total includes those cast by the Republic of China. The United States has used most of its vetoes to block resolutions it judged harmful to Israel, including two on Gaza in 2025. Rising vetoes are cited both by those who want the Council reformed to reflect today’s powers and by those who see a return of Cold War deadlock.
stats.source_label: Security Council Report, “Living with the Veto,” Research Report, March 2026

stats.label: Share of world population living in autocracies, 2025
stats.note: V-Dem estimates that 74 percent of the world’s people lived in autocracies at the end of 2025, up from 50 percent in 2005; some governments it classifies, including India’s, reject its labels.
stats.detail: The Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Institute at the University of Gothenburg codes every country’s political system from expert surveys. It counted 92 autocracies and 87 democracies at the end of 2025, put the share of people living in liberal democracies at 7 percent, down from 17 percent in 2005, and judged that the level of democracy experienced by the average person is back to where it was in 1978. Its 2026 report reclassified the United States as no longer a liberal democracy for the first time in over 50 years, citing the concentration of power in the presidency, a characterization the US administration rejects. The population shares are driven heavily by a few large countries, especially India, which V-Dem classifies as an electoral autocracy. This matters here because the “liberal” in the liberal order was partly a bet that democracy would keep spreading; the democratic backsliding page covers the domestic side.
stats.source_label: V-Dem Institute, Democracy Report 2026: Unraveling the Democratic Era?

stats.label: Fall in foreign aid from OECD donor countries, 2025
stats.note: Aid from the OECD’s donor countries fell 23.1 percent in real terms in 2025, to $174.3 billion, the largest one-year drop on record; US aid fell 56.9 percent.
stats.detail: Official development assistance is the grants and concessional loans governments give for development and humanitarian purposes, and it has long been a main channel of Western support to poorer countries. The 2025 fall was the second annual decline in a row and left aid at 0.26 percent of donors’ combined national income. The United States, which had been by far the largest donor, accounted for 75.1 percent of the fall after dismantling USAID, and the five largest donors, France, Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States, for 95.7 percent of it, as several European governments also cut aid to pay for defense. Those who see China gaining ground in the Global South point to this retreat; China’s own lending is not counted as aid in these figures.
stats.source_label: OECD, preliminary 2025 official development assistance data (April 9, 2026)

stats.label: Share of the UN regular budget assessed on the United States, 2025
stats.note: The United States is assessed 22 percent of the UN’s regular budget, the maximum allowed, and China 20.004 percent; China’s share was under 1 percent for most of the 1980s and 1990s.
stats.detail: UN dues are set every three years by a formula based mainly on each country’s share of world income, with a cap of 22 percent that only the United States reaches; the current scale runs from 2025 to 2027. Pew gives the 2025 amounts net of credits for countries that do not tax UN staff’s earnings: $820.4 million for the United States and $679.8 million for China, out of about $3.5 billion, so they do not scale exactly with the shares. China’s climb up the scale is one of the plainest institutional signs of its economic rise. Paying is a separate matter: the United States has long run arrears, and after paying $827 million in September 2026 it still owed about $4.2 billion, according to figures the UN spokesperson gave PassBlue. Voluntary funding for UN agencies, where the United States has historically been the largest donor, is not included in these shares.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, “How the United Nations is funded, and which countries pay the most” (July 31, 2025)

stats.label: Share of world population living in the ten BRICS members, 2024
stats.note: The ten BRICS members are home to about 48 percent of the world’s 8.14 billion people; the G7 countries to 9.6 percent and the United States to 4.2 percent.
stats.detail: Population is the plainest way to see why many governments call the post-1945 institutions unrepresentative, since their seats and voting weights were set when Europe and North America held a far larger share of the world’s people and output. Computed here from World Bank figures for 2024, the total counts BRICS as Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE and Indonesia; adding Saudi Arabia gives 48.5 percent. Population is not power by itself, and the most populous BRICS members are among its poorer ones per person, which is why those who doubt multipolarity point to income per head and technology rather than headcount.
stats.source_label: World Bank, World Development Indicators, Population, total; shares computed for this page

stats.label: Average US tariff rate, February 2025 and August 2026
stats.note: Yale’s Budget Lab puts the average US tariff rate at 11.0 percent in August 2026, against 2.4 percent at the start of February 2025, on two slightly different measures.
stats.detail: The rise since 2025 is the sharpest break with the open-trading rules the United States championed after 1945. The path has been uneven. On February 20, 2026, in Learning Resources v. Trump, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs, striking down the “reciprocal” tariffs; the administration replaced them with temporary tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act, which expired on July 24, 2026, and then with tariffs under Section 301. Yale projects the rate rising to 11.8 percent by the end of 2026 under current law. The August 2026 figure is Yale’s average statutory tariff rate; the February 2025 figure comes from its earlier average effective tariff rate series, which put the rate at 15.6 percent on June 1, 2025, so the comparison is approximate. Trade policy as such is covered on the free trade page.
stats.source_label: The Budget Lab at Yale, “The State of U.S. Tariffs” (August 24, 2026)

questions.text: Is the world already multipolar, or is the United States still the dominant power?
questions.why: The answer depends on what is counted: output at local prices or at market exchange rates, military reach, alliances, money, or the record of getting results. Both sides cite official data and disagree on which kinds of power decide outcomes.
questions.detail:
Those who see a multipolar world point to results. The United States could not stop Russia’s invasion of Ukraine or quickly end a war with Iran, and most of the world declined to join its sanctions on Russia. China out-builds the US Navy in hulls and leads in many clean-energy and manufacturing technologies, while India, the Gulf states, Turkey and Brazil act independently and play the great powers off against each other. Leaders who agree on little else, from the UN Secretary-General to India’s foreign minister and Canada’s prime minister, describe the shift as already under way.

Those who see the United States still on top say no other state combines its economy, military reach, treaty allies, technology, universities, energy independence and financial system, and that China has no comparable allies. The decline of “the West,” they argue, is mostly a decline of Europe and Japan, and China faces a shrinking, aging workforce, a property bust and heavy debt. On this reading the world is unipolar with a strong challenger, or at most bipolar, and what has changed is America’s choice about how to use its power.

questions.text: Did the US-led order deliver peace and prosperity for most of the world, or mainly serve its builders?
questions.why: The decades after 1945 saw no war between great powers and the fastest fall in poverty in history, but also US-led wars, coups and rules written mostly by rich countries. How much the order caused either is a counterfactual still argued over.
questions.detail:
Those who say it delivered credit its rules against conquest, open markets and security guarantees for the rise of postwar Germany and Japan, the East Asian economies, and the growth of China and India, which pulled more than a billion people out of extreme poverty by selling into Western markets. American alliances, they argue, ended the cycle of great-power war in Europe and Asia and kept nuclear weapons from spreading as widely as was predicted in the 1960s. Countries everywhere chose to join its institutions, and the rising powers now criticizing it grew rich inside it.

Those who say it served its builders answer that for much of the world the “rules-based order” meant rules made in Washington and applied selectively: Iraq invaded without Security Council approval, Libya bombed beyond the Council’s mandate, coups backed in Iran, Guatemala and Chile, and Israel shielded from Council action by repeated vetoes. Trade and intellectual-property rules favored rich exporters, IMF programs imposed austerity on borrowers, and the long peace among great powers coexisted with proxy wars across the Global South. Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, told Davos in January 2026 that the story was “partially false.”

questions.text: Would a world of several great powers be more dangerous than one led by the United States?
questions.why: Scholars have argued since the 1960s over whether one, two or several great powers make war likelier. History offers cases for each answer, and the recent rise in wars between states is too new for its causes to be settled.
questions.detail:
Those who expect more danger say that when no single power can enforce the peace, every state must look after itself, alliances shift and miscalculation grows likelier; that is how Europe stumbled into war in 1914. Several nuclear-armed powers with unsettled borders and competing spheres make crises more frequent and harder to manage, and they read the recent record in wars between states as an early sign. Robert Kagan, writing in The Atlantic in January 2026, argues that a return to nineteenth-century great-power politics brings a return to its wars.

Those who expect more stability answer that a single dominant power faces few checks, and that the unipolar years brought repeated US wars of choice. A balance forces each power to bargain, respect others’ core interests and avoid overreach, as the Concert of Europe did for decades after 1815, and nuclear weapons make direct war between great powers far less likely than in 1914. Many governments in Asia, Africa and Latin America also find that rivalry among several powers gives them more options and better terms than dependence on one.

questions.text: Should the United States keep paying to underwrite its allies’ security and the world’s institutions?
questions.why: For eighty years the United States has paid for alliances, troops abroad, aid and international bodies. Whether that bought American security or subsidized rich allies turns on weighing diffuse gains against concrete costs, and whom Washington serves first.
questions.detail:
Those who would keep underwriting call the order the best deal any great power ever had. It kept wars far from American shores, opened markets to US firms, let the dollar finance American deficits cheaply and turned former enemies into allies who fight alongside it. Its costs are small next to the US economy and far smaller than the wars it prevented. Pull back, they warn, and others fill the space: allies who cannot rely on Washington will hedge, rearm, seek nuclear weapons or make their own deals with Beijing and Moscow, leaving the United States less secure and poorer.

Those who would shift the burden say the costs look small only on a budget chart. Americans paid in taxes, debt and military service, and the commitments drew the country into long wars far from home; the wars the order supposedly prevented are a guess, while the ones it led to were real. Wealthy allies in Europe and Asia spent far less on defense for decades while relying on US protection. Even the dollar and open markets had a price: a currency kept strong by foreign demand and a market open to others’ exports helped hollow out American industry. Allies respond when pressed, and a United States that focuses on its own hemisphere and its own economy is stronger, not weaker.

questions.text: Can international rules hold without one dominant power to enforce them?
questions.why: Realists hold that rules last only while a strong state backs them; institutionalists hold that institutions keep working because members find them useful. The test is under way as the United States leaves some bodies and others decide whether to carry on.
questions.detail:
Those who think rules can hold note that most international rules work through reciprocity, not force: shipping, aviation, postal and telecommunications standards, most trade rules and the bulk of UN work. When Washington blocked appointments to the WTO’s appeals body, a group of members built an interim workaround. G. John Ikenberry argued in a February 2026 interview with the Asia Experts Forum that the liberal order is distinct from American hegemony and can outlast it, and most of the world wants predictable rules that middle powers can supply together.

Those who think rules need an enforcer reply that rules without enforcement are suggestions. The Security Council is paralyzed by vetoes, the WTO’s appeals body has lacked a quorum since December 2019, and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine showed how little the Charter’s ban on conquest means when a great power ignores it. Coalitions of middle powers cannot stop a determined great power, and without US naval and financial reach no one guarantees the sea lanes or punishes violators. Every past order, they argue, rested on a dominant state or a concert of strong ones; when Britain stepped back after 1918, the rules decayed and war followed.

questions.text: Should the international order promote democracy and human rights, or rest on sovereignty?
questions.why: The UN Charter promises sovereign equality and non-intervention; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights promises rights to every person. Whether an order should be built around free societies or coexistence among systems is a question of its purpose.
questions.detail:
Those who would promote democracy say rights are universal, not Western: the people of Hong Kong, Iran, Venezuela and Belarus who protested for them were not acting on foreign instructions. Democracies rarely fight each other and keep commitments more reliably, so an order of democracies is safer, while an order built only on sovereignty protects governments rather than people and gives cover to those who jail opponents, crush minorities or start wars. Dropping values, they add, throws away one of the strongest attractions the Western order had.

Those who put sovereignty first say every society has the right to choose its own path, and that the record of outsiders imposing democracy is one of chaos and death. Rights and democracy have been pressed against adversaries and rarely against allies, which is why much of the world sees them as tools of power, and a stable order among different systems requires agreeing to disagree about domestic politics. China’s Global Governance Initiative and the BRICS declarations put sovereign equality first, and the 2025 US National Security Strategy now promises good relations “without imposing on them democratic or other social change.”

questions.text: Does China want a bigger seat in the existing order, or a different order?
questions.why: China casts itself as the defender of the UN system and has joined most international institutions, but it has also built parallel ones, rejected a tribunal’s ruling and aligned with Russia. Its intentions are inferred from conduct that reads both ways.
questions.detail:
Those who see a bid for a bigger seat say China built its prosperity inside the existing order and has every reason to keep it working. It is a large contributor of UN peacekeepers and an active member of the WTO, IMF and World Bank, where it seeks larger voting shares rather than an exit, and its own institutions, such as the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, follow familiar multilateral rules and include many US allies. Its complaint that institutions underrepresent the countries where most people live is shared by India, Brazil and South Africa, and treating China as a revolutionary power risks making it one.

Those who see a bid for a different order say its actions say more than its documents. It rejected the 2016 arbitral ruling on the South China Sea, militarized artificial islands, threatens Taiwan, used trade bans to punish Australia and Lithuania, and has backed Russia’s war economy. Its idea of sovereign equality puts the authority of governments above individual rights and would keep the order’s shell while removing its liberal content, and its alternative payment systems and standards point toward an order in which Chinese power is secure from outside judgment.

questions.text: Should global institutions give rising powers more weight, even if the West loses control?
questions.why: The Security Council’s permanent seats and the IMF and World Bank votes reflect the world of 1945. Almost everyone backs reform in principle, but every plan takes power from someone, and those who would lose it doubt what more diverse majorities would protect.
questions.detail:
Those who would share power say institutions that much of humanity sees as unrepresentative cannot command loyalty, and that sharing control is the price of keeping them relevant. If they do not adapt, rising powers will keep building alternatives, as they already have with BRICS institutions, and the West will end up with less influence, not more. India’s foreign minister told the General Assembly in September 2026 that the case for reformed multilateralism “only gets stronger.”

Those who would reform gradually say the institutions work, where they work, because they are anchored by powers that pay for them and share broadly liberal commitments. Diluting that anchor without agreement on purposes risks paralysis or capture: more votes for authoritarian governments could turn bodies meant to protect rights and open markets into shields for repression and state-directed economics. The veto, for all its faults, keeps great powers inside the UN rather than outside it, and reform is better done in steps that rising powers earn by contributing.

positions.name: Renew the US-led rules-based order
positions.steelman: The order America built kept the great powers at peace for eighty years and opened the world to prosperity; it is being abandoned by choice, and it should be renewed, not mourned.
positions.detail:
Before 1945, great-power wars killed tens of millions. Afterward conquest became rare and costly, open markets lifted billions out of poverty, and smaller countries gained rules to appeal to and allies to rely on. It worked because the United States carried costs no other power would: guarding the sea lanes, extending a nuclear umbrella so that Germany, Japan and South Korea did not need their own bombs, and absorbing the imports that fueled others’ growth. A multipolar world is not a fairer world but a more dangerous one, the world of 1914 and 1939, in which strong states take what they can, small states suffer what they must, and authoritarian powers in Beijing and Moscow set the terms for their regions. So we would repair alliances, return to institutions and reform them from within, compete with China through coalitions of democracies, and make the open economy work better for those it left behind.

We are told the order was hypocritical, serving its builders and exempting them from its own rules. Its flaws are real, but they are reasons to fix it, not to replace it with something worse: no plausible alternative is less hypocritical, and rules applied unevenly still give weaker states a standing they lose in a world run by force. Countries joined American alliances and institutions far more often than the alternatives, and many in Asia want more US presence, not less, because of China. Some of us frame renewal as a contest of democracies against autocracies; others stress alliances and deterrence over democracy promotion.
positions.proponents: Robert Kagan; Atlantic Council; G. John Ikenberry; Biden administration

positions.name: Build a multipolar order with a fair say for rising powers
positions.steelman: The rules were written in 1945 by a few Western powers, when most of today’s countries were still colonies; a world that has risen deserves an order where its voice matches its weight.
positions.detail:
The order still bears its birthmarks: five permanent Security Council seats and none for Africa, Latin America or India; an IMF where one country can veto major decisions; rules enforced against the weak but not the strong. Multipolarity is not chaos but the democratization of international relations. The basis for a fair order already exists in the UN Charter: sovereign equality, non-interference and international law, applied to everyone rather than selectively. Unilateral sanctions, tariffs and military action without UN authority are the real threats to order. A world of several centers, each respecting the others’ political systems and paths of development, is fairer, and because no single power can impose its will, it is more likely to rest on genuine consensus.

Critics call multipolarity a slogan that shields authoritarian governments and point to Russia’s war in Ukraine. But the Charter’s ban on the use of force condemns aggression by anyone, and those critics have waged wars without UN approval and shielded Israel’s conduct in Gaza. We share a goal, not one vision. China calls for “an equal and orderly multipolar world,” in Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s words of March 2026. India seeks reformed multilateralism and a permanent Council seat, partners with the United States in the Quad while sitting in BRICS, and wants a multipolar Asia, not a China-led one. Brazil and South Africa stress development finance and representation. Russia’s claim to a sphere of influence over its neighbors is one that India, Brazil and many others among us do not endorse.
positions.proponents: Wang Yi; S. Jaishankar; Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva; BRICS; Vladimir Putin

positions.name: Put US interests first and bargain from strength
positions.steelman: The post-war order became a weapon used against us; America should use its unmatched power to win better deals, make allies carry their weight and put its own people first.
positions.detail:
After the Cold War, American elites convinced themselves that permanent domination of the whole world was in the national interest, and ordinary Americans paid: in wars that did not concern them, in a trade system that let China and others hollow out American industry, in defending rich allies who spent little on their own, and in membership of international bodies that oppose American interests and try to override American sovereignty. Other nations never stopped acting in their own interest. Our answer is neither isolation nor a new crusade. It is leverage, through tariffs, deals and, when necessary, force; leaving institutions that do not serve us; securing the Western Hemisphere first; and preventing any rival, above all China, from dominating regions vital to the United States. As the 2025 National Security Strategy puts it, “The days of the United States propping up the entire world order like Atlas are over.”

We are told this squanders the alliances and trust that multiplied American power and hands influence to China. But popularity is not power: allies stay because they need American protection and markets more than we need them, and they are finally paying their share, as NATO members showed when they committed at The Hague in 2025 to move toward 5 percent of GDP on defense. Within the camp, some would shift resources from Europe to deterring China in Asia, others want fewer commitments overall, and others are comfortable using force, as in Venezuela and Iran.
positions.proponents: Trump administration; Marco Rubio; JD Vance; Heritage Foundation

positions.name: Keep the rules alive through coalitions of middle powers
positions.steelman: The old order is not coming back, but a world where great powers do as they please is not the only alternative: together, middle powers can keep the rules alive.
positions.detail:
The rules-based order was always partly a useful fiction, in which the strongest exempted themselves when convenient, but it worked for countries like Canada, Finland, Japan or Chile because it gave them rules to rely on. Now the great powers, the United States included, use tariffs, finance and supply chains as weapons. We cannot restore American leadership and should not wait for it, but together we are large: the European Union and the Pacific trade pact that eleven countries completed after the United States walked away in 2017 can, with partners in Asia, Africa and Latin America, keep open trade, climate cooperation and collective security going. That means coalitions issue by issue, diversified trade, shared investment in defense, and respect for the Global South rather than lectures. As Mark Carney put it, “if you are not at the table, you are on the menu.” The aim is an order of many players, not of a few great powers.

We are told middle powers lack the military strength and unity to enforce anything, and that Europe still depends on American intelligence, nuclear deterrence and the dollar. That is a reason to build capacity, not to give up, and much of what the order provides, from trade rules and standards to health and climate cooperation, needs no military enforcement, only enough members to make the rules worth following. We still value NATO and keep the door open for Washington to return; we only refuse to let everything depend on one capital’s politics.
positions.proponents: Mark Carney; Alexander Stubb; European Policy Centre; Jacques Delors Institute

positions.name: Scale back US commitments and accept a balance of power
positions.steelman: A world of several great powers is normal, and America, behind two oceans, is safer in it than almost anyone; stop policing the world and let diplomacy do more than force.
positions.detail:
The unipolar moment was an accident of the Soviet collapse, and Washington misused it: expanding NATO to Russia’s borders, invading Iraq, toppling Libya’s government and trying to remake societies it did not understand. Those wars cost trillions of dollars and hundreds of thousands of lives without producing stable democracies. The sensible strategy is to let wealthy allies in Europe defend themselves, avoid wars of choice, negotiate with rivals over their core interests, and concentrate American power where it truly matters: preventing any single power from dominating a key region, which today means helping Asian states balance China. As Stephen Walt has argued, restoring unipolarity is probably impossible. This is neither isolationism nor America First militarism; it rejects both the liberal crusade and tariffs and raids as tools of dominance.

We are told restraint invites aggression, that Russia and China pressed forward when American resolve was doubted. But Russia’s invasion followed the NATO expansion realists had warned against for decades, so the lesson runs the other way. Restraint does not abandon the balance of power; it lets those most threatened carry most of the burden, and many of us reject spheres of influence in favor of negotiated settlements. We differ on China: offensive realists like John Mearsheimer would contain it hard in Asia, while others at the Quincy Institute favor détente.
positions.proponents: Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft; Stephen Walt; John Mearsheimer; Defense Priorities

crux.lead: Can common rules hold without one dominant power, and whom should a world order serve first?
crux.lead_highlight: common rules hold without one dominant power
crux.subtitle: Beneath the argument over how far power has shifted, the split runs two ways: whether institutions keep working when no single power backs them, and whether an order should protect individual rights and democracy, the equal sovereignty of states, or a nation’s own people first.
crux.empirical: Some of this can be watched over the next decade: whether wars between states keep rising as American commitments shrink or level off as new balances form; whether institutions keep working when their founder walks away; whether coalitions of middle powers deliver trade deals and defense on their own; whether a stronger China keeps the rules it endorses; and whether the dollar loses ground when it is used as a weapon.
crux.values: No data says who should write the rules or what they should protect. Someone who puts individual rights and democracy first sees no gain in spreading power among governments that jail their critics; someone who puts sovereign equality first sees liberal values as cover for domination. Nor can evidence weigh the risk of great-power war against a more even spread of power, or say if a country should pay to sustain an order that also serves others.

primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: a large desk globe on a curved stand as the dominant focal mass, showing simple rounded continent shapes; in front of it at medium scale, a round conference table with several plain empty chairs of equal size, the table's edge overlapping the base of the globe stand; a small container ship at the smallest scale on a curved band of sea in the foreground; the ground is a broad gentle curve; a dotted shipping route arcs across the whole frame from the ship around behind the globe as the connective element.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #6a62b0, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: flags, national emblems, eagles, dragons, bears, chess pieces, crowns, thrones, a single big chair or seat at the head of the table, scales, tug-of-war ropes, cracks, crumbling or broken globes, fire, missiles, tanks, soldiers, chains, arrows pointing up or down, dollar or currency signs, maps with labeled countries, pins on the map, handshakes.
